name: Zoe Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions or government. Your answers stay confidential. What does a normal workday look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I check the truck and switching sheet with my crew before sunrise, then we replace damaged fittings or restore a feeder after a fault. My apprenticeship taught me to trust a meter reading and the person holding the other end of a rope. I like leaving a street lit again, though the paperwork after a wet shift can eat the evening. My partner Jules handles school pickup when a callout runs late, and our two children have learned not to count on dinner at six.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew the software might tidy the forms, but somebody still has to make a dead line safe. I already use AI to draft plain summaries, and I check every technical detail myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mortgage is manageable and we have more than six months put away, so I’m not afraid of a quiet upgrade. I do worry that a neat-looking error in a work order might reach the truck unnoticed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’ll keep my present shifts and use the same paper cross-check on switching instructions. In the first year I’d ask our safety lead to log any bad AI summaries we catch, then bring those examples to the monthly crew meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly settled, with a small itch about people trusting a screen too quickly. A lineworker has to be allowed to say stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you show the crew at that meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A draft summary once called a damaged insulator a loose connector. I’d show the photo and the corrected form, because a real example travels further than a warning poster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would that change your family budget?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not in this picture. Jules and I would keep our mortgage payment and school spending as they are.

say: **Line repair** still needs a person to test and make the site safe.
**AI summaries** save a little office time, provided the crew checks them.
think: Our **mortgage cushion** lets us treat this as a work process issue.
A polished **work order** can hide a mistake that matters at the pole.
do: **Keep** current shifts and check switching sheets against site conditions.
**Bring** logged AI errors to the monthly crew meeting for a safety discussion.
feel: **Settled**, with a small worry about trusting software too readily.
S0.quote: A lineworker has to be allowed to say stop.
fieldNote: Her **savings** and higher pay make a small software change feel manageable.
She favours **crew review** because she has already caught a plausible error in an AI summary.

steps.text: Keep present line repair shifts and cross-check switching sheets
Bring logged AI summary errors to the monthly crew meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say the planners and call desk will feel this before the crews on the poles. We should let software shorten the paperwork, but keep the field crew in decisions about access and isolation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the office loses people, a bad route plan could land on us without anyone who knows the streets checking it. I’m on higher pay and there are other utilities hiring nearby, but I don’t want our safety margin quietly traded for speed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I’d ask to sit with the dispatch team and learn how their new planning tool handles faults. During the first year I’d take the company’s digital mapping course and ask our union safety group to review any new targets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Interested and a little on edge. I can learn a map system, but I can’t learn back a lost second checker after an accident.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which planning mistake would reach you first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A map could send our bucket truck down a lane too narrow for it. We would lose an hour before touching the damaged line, and customers would blame the crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why involve the union safety group?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The target affects every crew, not just me. I’d want our representatives to ask how much time the new route estimate leaves for isolation and testing.

say: **Dispatch** and customer calls change before physical line repair does.
**Crew judgment** must remain in access and safety decisions.
think: Fewer **office checkers** could push bad routes straight to the truck.
Nearby **utility jobs** give me choices, though unsafe targets would still hurt crews.
do: **Learn** the company’s digital fault map during the first year.
**Ask** union safety representatives to review new route and repair targets.
feel: **Interested** in tools, but uneasy about losing a second checker.
S1.quote: I can learn a map system, but I can’t learn back a lost second checker after an accident.
fieldNote: Her **adaptive streak** points toward the mapping course rather than a job search.
She carefully distinguishes **desk automation** from climbing and testing a live network.

steps.text: Take company digital mapping course for fault dispatch
Ask union safety group to review route and repair targets

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew the thinking software arrives first, and the hands-on robots are still about three years behind it. We have to keep repairing lines through that gap, even if the office changes overnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028, dispatch, diagrams and buying could be done by a system that barely needs us to explain a fault. Our pole work might last until roughly 2031, but I cannot count on my present pay after that; even our savings have a limit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d put aside a fixed part of each callout payment starting next month and ask payroll what training time the company will fund. If the company funds it, I’d train in network testing and robot oversight; in the first year after 2028 I’d apply for those duties while still taking repair shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious for the children’s routine more than for my pride. Three years sounds long until it is three school years and a mortgage statement every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much would you put aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jules and I could move one in five callout payments into savings without missing the mortgage. We would stop there if our school costs rose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the company will not fund the training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the other nearby utilities which roles take my apprenticeship before paying for a course myself. I will not spend the children’s buffer on a certificate with no actual job attached.

say: **Thinking AI** reaches dispatch first; line crews still have about three years before capable robots.
**Training access** should be offered to repair crews while their work still runs.
think: My **higher pay** may fall after the robots reach field repair around 2031.
Our **savings** buy time, but the mortgage keeps that time finite.
do: **Save** one fifth of callout pay while school costs allow.
**Seek** funded network testing and robot oversight training before applying for those duties after 2028.
feel: **Anxious** about school routines and a possible pay drop.
S2.quote: Three years sounds long until it is three school years and a mortgage statement every month.
fieldNote: She calculates a **callout saving** rule without treating existing savings as new saving.
Her **training plan** depends on employer funding and a real opening in network testing.

steps.text: Save one fifth of callout pay while school costs allow
Take funded network testing training if the company offers it
Apply for network testing duties after 2028 if qualified

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell our crew five years gives us room to shape the new safety rules before thinking AI arrives in 2031. The robots come around 2034, so I want apprentices to learn the old tests and the new machines together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’ll be close to fifty when the robots show up, with children heading toward expensive choices. That is enough time to qualify for a different technical role, but only if management stops treating future training as a poster on the wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask for a written training timetable this winter, then complete the company’s protection testing modules if they are funded. In the first year after 2031 I’d seek a testing post locally; if no post opens, I’d keep field shifts and apply at nearby utilities.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wary, but not cornered. A five-year runway is something I can work with if it has actual dates on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask management to put in writing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Course days, paid time, and whether a passed test makes me eligible for an opening. A vague training promise would not change our mortgage plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell an apprentice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d teach the hand checks as carefully as ever, then show how I verify a digital fault map. Apprentices should know which reading belongs to the actual wire.

say: **Five years** gives crews time to shape training and safety rules.
**Apprentices** should learn physical tests alongside future machines.
think: My **age** makes a credible technical move possible before robots arrive around 2034.
A **training poster** means little without paid days and eligible openings.
do: **Take** funded protection testing modules if the company provides paid time and a written timetable.
**Apply** for a local testing post after 2031 if qualified, then nearby utilities if needed.
feel: **Wary**, but able to act with a five-year runway.
S3.quote: A vague training promise would not change our mortgage plan.
fieldNote: She links **training** to paid time and a genuine vacancy.
Her **family costs** may rise as both children get older, so five years does not erase income risk.

steps.text: Take funded protection testing modules if company provides paid time
Apply for a local testing post if qualified after 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell friends a decade lets a company retire worn equipment and retrain crews in stages. I would still insist that the people who know the lines help write the robot safety rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At fifty-three when thinking AI arrives, I may choose fewer callouts, but I cannot assume we will have paid the mortgage off. A 2039 field robot is far enough away to plan, yet it could still squeeze the last years I intended to earn well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep my repair role now and review our mortgage balance with Jules each year. During the first year after 2036 I’d move into a testing or training role if one is offered at workable pay, and I’d help our union crew committee draft robot isolation rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Measured. I can picture a useful last stretch at work, though I want numbers before I call it a comfortable retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is workable pay for a new role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Enough to keep the mortgage payment and school or later study costs covered without drawing down our savings each month. I would compare the offer against my base pay, not the best callout year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should the robot rule say first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A crew member must verify isolation before any machine touches a line. A robot report alone should not clear a site for work.

say: **Staged training** and equipment changes suit a decade-long runway.
**Crew members** need a hand in robot isolation rules.
think: The **mortgage balance** may still matter when thinking AI arrives in 2036.
A **2039 robot** could trim my last high-pay years.
do: **Review** the mortgage balance with Jules each year.
**Move** to testing or training after 2036 only with workable pay.
**Draft** robot isolation rules through the union crew committee.
S4.quote: A robot report alone should not clear a site for work.
fieldNote: Her **long runway** makes gradual planning credible without assuming early retirement.
She requires **workable pay** before changing posts and keeps the family mortgage in view.

steps.text: Keep repair role while reviewing annual mortgage balance
Move to testing or training after 2036 if pay covers household costs
Draft robot isolation rules through union crew committee

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 picture worries me most, because the office could change before the crews have a route into other paid work. A funded training place with a real testing vacancy, plus clear safety rules, would help more than a speech.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who gets to stop a machine. The person standing at the line must keep that right.

portrait: **Zoe Moreau**, 43, is an experienced lineworker with a vocational certificate and apprenticeship who builds and repairs power lines.
She and partner Jules have **two school-age children**, a mortgage, higher pay and more than six months of savings.
She uses **AI daily** for draft summaries but checks technical facts against what the crew sees and measures.
Her **2028 fear** is that office automation outpaces funded training before field robots arrive around 2031.
With longer lead time, she seeks **paid testing work** and union safety rules while watching the mortgage balance.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most because thinking work changes before crews can secure paid training and other duties.
whatWouldHelp: A **funded training place** tied to a genuine testing vacancy would give her a route from field repair.
Clear **crew stop rules** would keep lineworkers able to halt unsafe robot work.
headlineQuote: The person standing at the line must keep that right.
